text:
Maya: Quick share — did a focused sweep on the streaming emit path. For short responses (<=6 tokens) we’re seeing worse perceived latency in the browser: p50 looks fine but p95/p99 for "first visible token" is up ~50–120ms compared to last week.

Ranjit: Can you paste the numbers and how you measured perceived latency?

Maya: Sure. Measured client-first-byte (CFB) vs server-first-send (SFS). Server SFS p95 ~ 28ms (unchanged). Client-perceived first token p95 jumped from 80ms -> 170ms on same hosts. So the delay is after server emits — seems related to chunk/emit cadence + how the client buffers.

Leo: Interesting — could be aggregation on the network or our HTTP chunk framing. Any changes in kernel selection or batching config recently?

Maya: There was a runtime kernel-selection tweak last deploy (commit d4f2b1c) that altered small-seq codepath ordering. Microprofile shows extra memcpy/serialize time right before the emit call for small sequences. Stack excerpt:

```
serialize_tokens()  3.4ms
prepare_emit_batch() 4.8ms
grpc_stream_send_chunk() 9.2ms
client_write_flush()  0.7ms
```

The weird bit: when autoscaler/auto-batcher groups tiny requests we end up waiting for the batch window before the network emit, but when we short-circuit (fast-lane) the kernel, the kernel warmup/copy adds overhead. So two opposing sources of latency.

Sasha: TLDR: batching delay vs kernel warmup/copy delay. Batch to amortize overhead vs immediate small-host kernel overhead.

Ranjit: Got it. Do we know what the current emit cadence is? i.e., flush interval and chunk size?

Maya: Current default is `stream.emit_interval_ms = 60` and `stream.emit_max_tokens = 12`. I ran an A/B in canary with 30ms / 6-token vs 90ms / 24-token. Measurements: the 30ms config improved perceived p95 for 1–6 token responses by ~60ms but increased total CPU overhead by ~8% and reduced aggregate throughput by ~6% under high QPS.

Leo: So there's a clear tradeoff: lower latency for short responses at the cost of throughput/cost. Maybe we should adapt based on predicted response length.

Maya: Yep — I prototyped a predictive flush: if model outputs expected tokens <= 8, use emit_interval_ms 20 + fast-lane kernel. Otherwise use default batching. Prototype config snippet: 

```
"stream": {
  "emit_interval_ms": 60,
  "emit_max_tokens": 12,
  "fast_lane": {
    "enable": true,
    "emit_interval_ms": 20,
    "max_predicted_tokens": 8
  }
}
```

Ranjit: How accurate is the prediction? We’d need a cheap predictor at request time (maybe next-token entropy heuristic or prefix token count). False positives will cost throughput.

Maya: I used a simple heuristic: if prompt contains the word "summary" or template is within short-template set OR previous avg response length for this route < 10, route to fast-lane. Accuracy ~78% on our production traces for the test routes.

Sasha: We also need to consider KV cache behavior. If fast-lane forces a different kernel choice it may bypass some cache reuse patterns and actually increase p99 for long requests that share KV state. Did you see cache miss rate changes?

Maya: Good call — I saw KV-hit ratio drop ~3% in canary for mixed traffic. The fast-lane path recompiled a slightly different kernel (no fused memcpy) which caused a new codepath with separate cache keys in our profiler. So there’s also a longer-term cost in cold-cache scenarios.

Leo: Might be worth improving kernel selection to keep the same cache key for both paths. E.g., expose a lightweight flag to the kernel selector: treat fast-lane and normal-lane as cache-compatible when shapes match.

Maya: Agreed. I filed RFC PR #412 to add a "cache_compat=true" hint to kernel selection so the KV entries unify.

Ranjit: For rollout plan — recommend a canary: 5% traffic with adaptive flush + cache_compat hint. Measure perceived p95/p99, CPU %, throughput, KV hit rate. If KV-hit impact >1% revert. Also add a throttling guard on fast-lane when overall QPS > X to avoid throughput collapse.

Maya: Will do. Perf numbers I recorded (summary):
• baseline: perceived p95 = 170ms, p99 = 330ms, cpu util = 62%
• fast-lane w/o cache-compat: p95 = 110ms, p99 = 230ms, cpu util = 70%, kv-hit -3%
• adaptive with larger batch window: p95 = 150ms, p99 = 290ms, cpu util = 64%

Sasha: Also add metrics for client-visible first-token latency (separate from server-send) — we need both for SLOs. And track tail latencies per route since some templates are more sensitive.

Maya: Yep adding histograms and route tags. I’ll add an experiment to collect `client_first_token_ms` and `server_send_ms` and ship to the console dashboard.

perf-bot: Benchmark job queued: `bench/streaming/fastlane-smoke` (canary-5pct) — started.

Leo: One more nit — we should test with real browser clients; some browsers buffer tiny chunks and don't render until a certain threshold. We might need to co-tune chunk size with SSE/HTTP headers (e.g., `X-Chunk-Mode: flush-immediate`).

Maya: Noted. I’ll run a small client-compatibility matrix across Chrome/Firefox/Safari.

Sasha: Action items:
- Maya: land kernel cache_compat hint + fast-lane config PR (create draft)
- Ranjit: add canary gating + throttle guard in router
- Leo: plan client-browser tests and tweak headers
- Maya: telemetry (client_first_token_ms, kv-hit-rate, cpu, throughput) on console dashboards

Maya: Thanks — will push a draft PR and follow up with data in this thread. :eyes: (reaction: :thumbsup:)

ci-bot: PR #418 created by Maya: `streaming: fast-lane adaptive emit + kernel cache hint (draft)`

Ranjit: Nice. Once PR is up, assign perf review and we’ll schedule the 5% canary for tomorrow.

Maya: Will do, thanks!
